pages.subtitle: The "Way of Sorrows" through Jerusalem, where Christians pray the Stations of the Cross.

quick_facts.label: Bible event
quick_facts.value: Jesus carries his cross to Calvary

quick_facts.label: First church built
quick_facts.value: Not a church: a prayer route, set in the 1700s

quick_facts.label: Cared for by
quick_facts.value: Franciscans lead prayer along it every Friday

pages.intro: The Via Dolorosa is a route through the narrow streets of Jerusalem's Old City. Its name means "the Way of Sorrows." Christians walk it to remember Jesus carrying his cross to Calvary. Along the way are fourteen Stations of the Cross. The last five are inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where Jesus died and rose again.
story_paragraphs: After Jesus was arrested, he was brought before Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate had Jesus whipped, and soldiers put a crown of thorns on his head. Then Pilate brought Jesus out to the crowd and said, "Behold, the man!" The crowd shouted for Jesus to be crucified, and Pilate handed him over.

Jesus carried his cross out of the city toward a hill called Golgotha. The Gospels tell us that the soldiers made a man named Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, carry the cross behind Jesus. A large crowd followed, including women who were weeping for him. Jesus turned and spoke to them with love, even in his suffering.
At Golgotha, Jesus was crucified. He died, was buried, and on the third day he rose from the dead.

From the earliest centuries, Christians in Jerusalem walked and prayed along the way they believed Jesus had taken. Over time, this became the prayer called the Stations of the Cross. Today, Catholics all over the world pray the Stations in their own parish churches, especially during Lent.

The route we call the Via Dolorosa today was set in the 1700s. It begins near the Lions' Gate and winds west through the busy streets of the Old City. Nine stations are along the street, marked by small signs and chapels. The last five are inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

Every Friday afternoon, Franciscan friars lead people in praying the Stations along the Via Dolorosa. Neighbors, workers and pilgrims from many countries share the narrow streets with them, just as the crowds did on the day Jesus walked to Calvary.

pages.subtitle: The church in Jerusalem where, by tradition, Mary "fell asleep" at the end of her life on earth.

quick_facts.label: Bible event
quick_facts.value: Mary with the apostles in Jerusalem; by tradition, the end of her life on earth

pages.intro: On Mount Zion in Jerusalem, near the Upper Room, stands a big round church with a tall bell tower. It is called Dormition Abbey. "Dormition" means "falling asleep." By an old tradition, this is where Mary, the Mother of Jesus, came to the end of her life on earth. Catholics believe that God then took Mary, body and soul, into heaven.
story_paragraphs: As Jesus was dying on the cross, he saw his mother, Mary, standing nearby with the disciple John. Jesus said to Mary, "Woman, behold, your son." Then he said to John, "Behold, your mother." From that hour, John took Mary into his home.

After Jesus rose from the dead and returned to his Father in heaven, the apostles gathered in Jerusalem to pray. The Acts of the Apostles tells us that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was with them. She prayed with the first Christians as they waited for the Holy Spirit.

The Bible does not tell us what happened to Mary at the end of her life. But Christians have long remembered that she "fell asleep" peacefully, surrounded by love. The Church teaches that when Mary's life on earth was finished, God took her, body and soul, into the glory of heaven. This is called the Assumption, and Catholics celebrate it every year on August 15.
An old tradition says that Mary lived her last days on Mount Zion. In the 300s, a great church called Hagia Sion was built there. It was called "the Mother of all Churches." It was destroyed in 614.
In 1898, the land was given to the German emperor, Wilhelm II, who presented it to the Catholic Church. The new church was finished in 1910. Benedictine monks live there and pray in it every day.
In the lower church, called the crypt, there is a life-size statue of Mary lying peacefully asleep. Above her, the dome shows Jesus with his arms open, welcoming his mother into heaven.

pages.student_title: The Church of the Pater Noster
pages.subtitle: The church on the Mount of Olives where Christians remember Jesus teaching the Our Father, written on its walls in many languages.
pages.intro: On the Mount of Olives, looking out over Jerusalem, is a church with a quiet courtyard whose walls are covered with colorful tiles. Each tile shows the Our Father, the prayer Jesus taught us, in a different language. There are about 140 of them! "Pater Noster" is Latin for "Our Father." Christians remember this as a place where Jesus taught his disciples.
story_paragraphs: Jesus often went out to the Mount of Olives, a hill just east of Jerusalem, to pray and to teach his disciples.

One day, Jesus was praying. When he finished, one of his disciples said, "Lord, teach us to pray." So Jesus taught them a prayer: "Father, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come." He taught them to ask God for their daily bread, for forgiveness, and for help in times of trial.

In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus gives this prayer as part of his great teaching on the mountain. He says, "This is how you are to pray: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name." We still pray these words today, at every Mass and in the Rosary. We call it the Our Father, or the Lord's Prayer.
The Gospels also tell us that Jesus taught his disciples on the Mount of Olives about the end of time, and that from near this hill he returned to his Father in heaven.

Around the year 330, Emperor Constantine built a large church here, over a cave where Christians remembered Jesus teaching. It was called the Eleona, from the Greek word for "olive grove." Later, the Crusaders built a church here and called it Pater Noster, Latin for "Our Father."

In the 1800s, a French princess, Aurélie de Bossi, bought the land. She built a church and a cloister, and she put up the Our Father in many languages. She also built a convent for Carmelite sisters, who still live and pray there.
Today, the Our Father appears on the walls in about 140 languages, from English and Spanish to Swahili, Hawaiian and Korean. It is a beautiful reminder that God is the Father of people everywhere.

pages.student_title: The Tomb of Lazarus in Bethany
pages.subtitle: The town where Jesus visited his friends Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and called Lazarus out of the tomb.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: Bethany, on the Mount of Olives

quick_facts.label: Bible event

quick_facts.label: Cared for by
quick_facts.value: Catholic Franciscans care for the church

pages.intro: Bethany is a small town on the far side of the Mount of Olives, near Jerusalem. Jesus had three close friends there: Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus. When Lazarus died, Jesus wept. Then he called, "Lazarus, come out!" and Lazarus walked out of his tomb alive. People still go down the steps into the rock tomb that tradition remembers as his.
story_paragraphs: Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, who lived in the village of Bethany. He often stayed at their home.

One day, Lazarus became very sick. His sisters sent a message to Jesus: "Master, the one you love is ill." By the time Jesus arrived in Bethany, Lazarus had died and had been in the tomb for four days.

Martha ran out to meet Jesus. Jesus told her, "I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live." Martha answered, "Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God."
Then Mary came and fell at Jesus' feet, crying. When Jesus saw her weeping, and the friends weeping with her, he was deeply moved. The Bible says, "Jesus wept." He loved his friend very much.

Jesus went to the tomb, a cave with a stone across it. He told them to take the stone away. He prayed to his Father. Then he cried out in a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" And Lazarus came out, still wrapped in burial cloths. Jesus said, "Untie him and let him go."
Many people who saw this believed in Jesus. A few days later, Jesus went up to Jerusalem for the Passover, where he would die and rise again.

By the 300s, Christians were coming to Bethany to pray at the tomb of Lazarus, and a church was built nearby. Today, a Franciscan church built in 1954 stands beside it. It is sometimes called the Sanctuary of Friendship. The Arabic name of the town, al-Azariya, comes from the name Lazarus.

pages.student_title: The Church of the Visitation in Ein Karem
pages.subtitle: The church in a hillside village where Christians remember Mary visiting her relative Elizabeth and singing the Magnificat.

quick_facts.label: Bible event
quick_facts.value: Mary visits Elizabeth and sings the Magnificat

quick_facts.label: First church built
quick_facts.value: Remembered here from the 500s; today's church finished in 1955

pages.intro: Ein Karem is a pretty village in the hills west of Jerusalem. Here, Christians remember the day Mary, who was expecting Jesus, hurried to visit her relative Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby in Elizabeth's womb, John the Baptist, leaped for joy. Mary answered with a song of praise called the Magnificat, which is written on the church walls in many languages.
story_paragraphs: After the angel Gabriel visited Mary in Nazareth, he told her some other surprising news. Her relative Elizabeth, who was old, was going to have a baby too. Nothing is impossible for God!

Mary set out at once and traveled to a town in the hill country of Judea to visit Elizabeth. When Mary came into the house and greeted her, Elizabeth's baby leaped inside her. Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. She cried out, "Most blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb." We still pray these words in the Hail Mary.

Mary answered with a beautiful song of praise: "My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord; my spirit rejoices in God my savior." This song is called the Magnificat, from its first word in Latin. In it, Mary praises God for lifting up the lowly and filling the hungry with good things.
Mary stayed with Elizabeth for about three months. Then Elizabeth's son was born. His father, Zechariah, named him John. He grew up to be John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus.
By the 500s, Christians remembered Ein Karem as the place where Elizabeth lived. Churches were built here over the centuries. The Franciscans began restoring the holy places here in 1679.

The Church of the Visitation that stands today was designed by Antonio Barluzzi and finished in 1955. In its courtyard, the Magnificat is written on tiles in more than 40 languages. Down the hill is a spring called Mary's Spring, and in the village is another church that remembers the birth of John the Baptist.
